title: Should You Ask Team Members to Read Before Discussions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece describes Amazon's practice, championed by Jeff Bezos and continued under Andy Jassy, of replacing slide decks with six-page memos that meeting attendees read silently together before discussing. It explains the rationale: reading together avoids skimming, keeps information fresh, and surfaces weak thinking through the discipline of writing a complete, logical case. The article suggests other leaders experiment with the model on at least one high-stakes issue, framing rigorous shared understanding as the real driver of long-term organizational success.
points: Amazon replaced slide decks with six-page memos read silently together at the start of meetings.
Bezos insisted on group reading, not pre-reading, to keep information fresh and avoid skimming.
Andy Jassy credits the writing process with teaching him to think through and present ideas logically.
The article suggests trialing the practice on a single high-stakes decision as a low-risk experiment.
quotes: Former Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos detested slide deck presentations because they too often allowed for a superficial overview and discussion of the issues involved in a critical project or decision.
At the start of meetings, attendees spend about 30 minutes in silence reading the memo, creating a deep understanding of the issues.
Unlike similar organizations with critical decisions to make, leaders at Amazon spend between one and four hours writing and reading every day.
Current CEO Andy Jassy credits this writing process with teaching him how to thoroughly consider ideas and to present them logically for others.
Perhaps attempting the six-page memo and silent reading on one critical issue would prove a valuable experiment.
